case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, under the PSLRA, securities-fraud plaintiffs can plead falsity and scienter without particularized factual allegations—by relying on generalized accounts of internal documents and/or an expert opinion in place of specific facts.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 (PSLRA), especially 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(b)(1) (pleading falsity with particularity) and § 78u-4(b)(2)(A) (pleading scienter with particularity and a “strong inference”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: NVIDIA argues the Ninth Circuit diluted the PSLRA’s heightened pleading rules by allowing plaintiffs to (1) assert scienter based on supposed internal company documents without pleading their contents with particularity, and (2) satisfy falsity by substituting an expert’s say-so for particularized factual allegations. Petitioners contend Congress enacted the PSLRA to screen out weak “nuisance” securities class actions before discovery and settlement pressure, so plaintiffs must identify specific contradictory facts (including what internal documents actually said, when, and how they conflict with the challenged public statements) and must plead facts—rather than expert conclusions—to establish falsity and a strong inference of scienter.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue the complaint satisfies the PSLRA because it pleads enough particularized facts to make falsity and scienter plausible and “strongly” inferable, and that the PSLRA does not impose an inflexible requirement to quote or reproduce internal documents at the pleading stage. They maintain expert analysis can be used to explain technical subject matter and support the pleaded factual theory of falsity (rather than improperly replacing facts), and that NVIDIA’s proposed rule would improperly raise the bar beyond the statute and effectively require discovery-level detail before plaintiffs can access discovery.
key_precedents: Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith Inc. v. Dabit, 547 U.S. 71 (2006)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that the PSLRA contains no verbatim-quotation requirement and that we should avoid an extra-textual rule that effectively demands discovery at the pleading stage. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Alito emphasize, the statute still requires plaintiffs to “specify” the challenged statements and plead “with particularity” the facts showing why they were misleading and supporting a Tellabs “strong inference” of scienter; vague invocations of internal materials or an expert’s bottom-line conclusion, without document-specific content, timing, and contradiction, deprive courts of a workable basis to perform Tellabs’s comparative inference analysis. Under a minimalist approach, the narrow holding is simply that no categorical quotation mandate exists, yet the complaint must allege enough concrete detail about the internal information to test falsity and scienter without shifting the PSLRA’s gatekeeping function into discovery. That accommodates access concerns without weakening Congress’s screening design, especially given the discovery stay.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s access-to-documents concern does not justify relaxing the PSLRA’s text: Congress required plaintiffs to “specify” each statement and “the reason or reasons why,” and to “state with particularity” the “facts” supporting falsity and a “strong inference” of scienter—requirements not met by generalized descriptions of unnamed internal materials or an expert’s bottom-line conclusion. As Justice Kagan explains, this is not an extra-textual verbatim-quotation rule; it is simply insisting on enough pleaded content, timing, and contradiction to make Tellabs’s comparative-inference analysis possible. The discovery stay is part of the statutory design, and reading “particularity” to allow vague summaries would effectively shift the PSLRA’s screening function from pleading to discovery, contrary to the enacted scheme. Because § 10(b) is judicially implied, we should be especially faithful to Congress’s gatekeeping terms rather than dilute them in the name of flexibility.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that the PSLRA does not impose a verbatim-quotation requirement, and we should not create an inflexible “quote it or lose” rule that functions as a disguised discovery mandate. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, the statutory demands to “specify” each misleading statement and to “state with particularity facts” supporting falsity and a “strong inference” of scienter are not met by generalized references to unnamed internal documents or an expert’s bottom-line conclusion untethered to concrete pleaded content, timing, and contradiction. Without those particulars, Tellabs’s comparative-inference analysis becomes largely unworkable and the discovery stay’s gatekeeping function is undermined in precisely the way Congress sought to prevent. A narrow rule requiring document-specific substance (not verbatim quotation) best fits the text, the PSLRA’s design, and practical administrability.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan rightly stress that Tellabs is difficult to apply if a complaint offers only vague invocations of “internal documents” or an expert’s bottom-line conclusion; I agree courts should require concrete contextual allegations (what the report concerned, when, who saw it, and how it conflicted with the public statement). But Justice Thomas’s and Justice Barrett’s push to treat anything short of pleading the pertinent contents in near-document form as not “facts” risks converting the PSLRA’s particularity requirement into a practical impossibility given the discovery stay and defendants’ exclusive control over internal materials. Under Tellabs’s holistic approach, sufficiently detailed summaries plus expert explanation of technical meaning can contribute to a strong inference of scienter so long as they are anchored to specific contradictions and timing, without importing an extra-textual quasi-quotation mandate. The administrable line is not “quote it,” but “plead enough linkage and detail to test contradiction and competing inferences,” and I would not adopt a rule that functionally immunizes concealed fraud from any pre-discovery challenge.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to resist an extra-textual, categorical “quote-the-document” rule, and I would not endorse anything that effectively requires discovery-level access at pleading. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, the PSLRA’s commands to “specify” each statement, plead “the reason or reasons why,” and “state with particularity facts” supporting a “strong inference” of scienter require enough concrete content—what the internal information conveyed, when, and how it contradicts the challenged statements—to make Tellabs’s comparative-inference analysis workable. An expert can explain technical significance, but cannot substitute for particularized factual allegations about the underlying contradictory information; otherwise the complaint becomes a bottom-line conclusion that shifts the PSLRA’s gatekeeping from pleading to discovery, in tension with the statute’s discovery stay and coherent design. A narrow, administrable holding—no verbatim-quotation mandate, but a requirement of document-specific and contradiction-specific factual detail—best fits the text and preserves flexibility without collapsing particularity into generalities.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that the PSLRA does not demand verbatim quotation of internal documents, and I would reject any “quote it or lose” rule for that reason. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, the statute’s command to “state with particularity facts” and to “specify” the reasons a statement was misleading is not satisfied by vague allusions to undisclosed materials or an expert’s bottom-line conclusion; without pleading the pertinent substance, timing, and concrete contradiction, courts cannot perform Tellabs’s comparative-inference analysis in any meaningful way. Justice Jackson’s access-to-documents concern is real, yet Congress paired heightened pleading with a discovery stay, and our job is to enforce that gatekeeping design rather than dilute “facts” and “particularity” into generalized characterizations. Properly framed, the rule is flexible (no verbatim requirement) but still demands enough document-specific detail to test falsity and scienter at the pleading stage.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that the PSLRA does not impose a verbatim-quotation rule and we should not convert pleading into discovery, especially given defendants’ control of internal documents. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the statute still requires plaintiffs to plead particularized “facts” explaining why specified statements were misleading and supporting a “strong inference” of scienter; vague references to internal materials or an expert’s bottom-line conclusion are not enough for Tellabs’s comparative-inference analysis to function. A workable, text-faithful middle position is to require plaintiffs to plead the substance of the internal information with specificity—contents, timing, recipients, and concrete contradiction—without demanding verbatim excerpts. That approach enforces Congress’s screening design (including the discovery stay) while avoiding the extra-textual rigidity Sotomayor warns against.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s access-to-documents concern is serious, but it does not overcome the PSLRA’s textual demand that a plaintiff “state with particularity” the “facts” showing why specified statements were misleading and supporting a “strong inference” of scienter; generalized references to internal materials, untethered to their pertinent contents and timing, are not pleaded “facts” in the statutory sense. Chief Justice Roberts is right that the discovery stay makes pleading the gatekeeping device, so letting an expert’s bottom-line conclusion substitute for concrete contradictions would effectively shift the PSLRA’s screening function from the complaint to discovery. Justice Kagan’s middle-ground framing best answers the strongest opposing argument: we need not impose a verbatim-quotation rule, but we may require allegations that meaningfully describe what the internal information said, when it was known, and how it concretely conflicted with the public statements so that Tellabs’s comparative-inference analysis is actually possible. Under an originalist/textualist approach, that rule enforces Congress’s chosen specificity threshold without adding an extra-textual quotation requirement or granting defendants “immunity.”

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan rightly emphasize workability under Tellabs: courts need enough content, timing, and linkage to weigh competing inferences, and purely vague invocations of “internal documents” or an expert’s bottom-line cannot do that. But their administrability concern is best handled by enforcing a contextual specificity requirement within the PSLRA’s text—not by effectively demanding pleaded contents at a level that, in practice, becomes a discovery substitute given the PSLRA stay and defendants’ exclusive control of internal materials. Justice Thomas’s nuisance-suit screening point is substantial, yet a rule that treats non-verbatim summaries or expert-supported technical explanations as categorically insufficient risks insulating concealed misconduct and undermines procedural fairness when plaintiffs plausibly plead concrete contradictions (who, when, what metrics, and how inconsistent). Under a pragmatic approach attentive to real-world pleading constraints, I would affirm a flexible particularity standard that filters conclusory complaints while preserving meritorious claims where the alleged contradictions and scienter inference are coherently pleaded in context.

John Roberts.reasoning: The PSLRA requires that a complaint “specify each statement alleged to have been misleading” and “the reason or reasons why,” 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(b)(1), and that it “state with particularity facts” giving rise to a “strong inference” of scienter, § 78u-4(b)(2)(A). Under Tellabs, that inference must be “cogent and at least as compelling as any opposing inference,” 551 U.S. 308, 314 (2007), which is difficult to assess where the complaint relies on generalized descriptions of internal documents or an expert’s conclusion rather than particularized factual allegations about what the documents said, when, and how they contradict the challenged statements. Given Congress’s evident purpose to screen weak claims before discovery pressure (reinforced by the discovery stay, § 78u-4(b)(3)(B)), a narrow ruling requiring more concrete, particularized allegations—without demanding discovery-level proof—best aligns with the statutory text and preserves institutional legitimacy by enforcing the line Congress drew.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The PSLRA’s text demands particularity: a complaint must “specify each statement alleged to have been misleading” and “the reason or reasons why” it was misleading, 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(b)(1), and must “state with particularity facts giving rise to a strong inference” of scienter, § 78u-4(b)(2)(A). Allowing plaintiffs to rely on generalized descriptions of supposed internal documents, without pleading what those documents actually said and how they contradict the challenged statements, dilutes Congress’s heightened pleading threshold and invites the very discovery-driven “nuisance” suits the statute was enacted to curb. Under Tellabs, the scienter inference must be “cogent and at least as compelling as any opposing inference of nonfraudulent intent,” 551 U.S. 308, 314 (2007), a comparative inquiry that cannot be satisfied by conclusory expert say-so in lieu of particularized facts. Because this is a judicially implied private right under § 10(b), it must be construed narrowly, and the PSLRA’s specific pleading commands should be enforced as written.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The PSLRA’s text requires that a complaint “specify each statement alleged to have been misleading” and “the reason or reasons why the statement is misleading,” and, for scienter, “state with particularity facts giving rise to a strong inference” of the required state of mind. 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(b)(1), (b)(2)(A). Allowing plaintiffs to rely on generalized descriptions of internal documents—without pleading their contents and the specific contradictions to the challenged public statements—and to substitute an expert’s conclusions for particularized facts would dilute Congress’s heightened gatekeeping regime designed to prevent discovery-driven “nuisance” suits and settlement pressure. Under Tellabs, courts must weigh competing inferences, and a complaint built on vague internal-document accounts and expert say-so will rarely yield an inference of scienter that is “cogent and at least as compelling as any opposing inference of nonfraudulent intent.” 551 U.S. 308, 314 (2007).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The PSLRA requires plaintiffs to “state with particularity all facts” supporting falsity and to plead “facts giving rise to a strong inference” of scienter, 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(b)(1), (b)(2)(A), but it does not, by its text, impose an inflexible rule that internal documents must be quoted or reproduced verbatim at the pleading stage. Under Tellabs, the court must evaluate whether the pleaded facts—taken collectively—support a scienter inference that is “cogent and at least as compelling” as nonfraudulent explanations, 551 U.S. 308, 314 (2007), and generalized descriptions of internal reports may contribute to that holistic inference where they are pled with sufficient contextual detail. Expert analysis likewise may assist in explaining technical matters and linking particularized allegations to falsity, so long as it does not substitute for facts altogether; adopting petitioners’ categorical rule would risk converting the PSLRA’s heightened pleading standard into a de facto discovery prerequisite, undermining access to justice for investors without meaningfully advancing the statute’s screening function.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The PSLRA’s text requires plaintiffs to “specify each statement alleged to have been misleading” and “the reason or reasons why,” § 78u-4(b)(1), and to “state with particularity facts giving rise to a strong inference” of scienter, § 78u-4(b)(2)(A); generalized references to unnamed internal documents or an expert’s bottom-line opinion cannot substitute for particularized factual allegations showing what the documents said and how they directly contradict the challenged statements. Tellabs reinforces that scienter allegations must yield an inference that is “cogent and at least as compelling as any opposing inference” of nonfraudulent intent, which is difficult to do when the complaint relies on vague summaries rather than concrete, specified facts. A rule allowing expert say-so or generalized document descriptions to carry the pleading burden would undercut Congress’s screening function and the discovery stay by effectively permitting plaintiffs to use pleadings to access discovery to find the needed particulars. This reading best preserves statutory coherence and workability across § 78u-4(b)(1) and (b)(2) without imposing an extra-textual quotation requirement, while still demanding the kind of specificity Congress required.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The PSLRA’s text requires plaintiffs to “specify each statement alleged to have been misleading” and “the reason or reasons why the statement is misleading,” 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(b)(1), and to “state with particularity facts giving rise to a strong inference” of scienter, § 78u-4(b)(2)(A). Allowing generalized descriptions of unnamed internal documents (without pleading their contents, timing, and contradiction) or an expert’s conclusions to substitute for “facts” dilutes the statute’s particularity command and invites the very pre-discovery fishing expeditions Congress sought to curb. Under Tellabs, the pleaded facts must yield a scienter inference “cogent and at least as compelling as any opposing inference,” 551 U.S. at 314, and without document-specific allegations the nonfraudulent inference (benign or mistaken assessment) will typically remain at least as strong. Consistent with the PSLRA’s plain meaning and separation-of-powers concerns about using discovery to manufacture claims, the complaint must stand or fall on particularized factual allegations, not expert say-so or vague invocations of internal materials.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The PSLRA requires plaintiffs to “state with particularity all facts” supporting falsity and to plead “facts giving rise to a strong inference” of scienter, 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(b)(1), (2)(A), and Congress enacted those heightened standards to prevent discovery-driven, nuisance suits. Under Tellabs, courts must assess scienter by weighing competing inferences from the pleaded facts; generalized allegations that unspecified internal documents contradicted public statements, or expert conclusions untethered to particularized facts, do not supply the concrete factual basis needed to draw a “strong inference” at the motion-to-dismiss stage. Consistent with institutional concerns and statutory text, the more workable rule is that plaintiffs must plead the pertinent contents of the internal materials (what they said, when, and how they conflicted) and must use expert analysis only to explain technical matters, not to substitute for the particularized facts the statute demands.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The PSLRA’s text requires plaintiffs to “specify each statement alleged to have been misleading” and “the reason or reasons why the statement is misleading,” § 78u-4(b)(1), and to “state with particularity facts giving rise to a strong inference” of scienter, § 78u-4(b)(2)(A). Generalized references to internal documents—without pleading their contents, timing, and concrete contradiction of the challenged statements—do not satisfy the statute’s demand for particularized facts, especially given the discovery stay that makes pleading the principal gatekeeping device. Nor can an expert’s conclusory opinion substitute for pleaded facts establishing falsity; at most, expert analysis may explain technical matters once the complaint has alleged particularized contradictory facts. Under Tellabs, the scienter inference must be “cogent and at least as compelling as any opposing inference,” 551 U.S. 308, 314 (2007), and a complaint built on vague “internal documents” and expert say-so typically cannot meet that comparative, strong-inference standard.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The PSLRA requires plaintiffs to “specify each statement alleged to have been misleading” and “the reason or reasons why” it was misleading, and to plead facts supporting a “strong inference” of scienter. 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(b)(1), (b)(2)(A). But nothing in the statute imposes an inflexible rule that internal documents must be quoted or reproduced verbatim at the pleading stage, and expert analysis may permissibly explain technical matters so long as it supports—rather than substitutes for—particularized factual allegations of falsity. Consistent with Tellabs, courts should weigh competing inferences and dismiss only when the pleaded facts do not make a cogent inference of scienter at least as compelling as an innocent explanation; a categorical bar on generalized document descriptions or expert-supported pleading risks converting the PSLRA into a discovery-level pleading regime with harsh practical consequences for meritorious claims and equal enforcement of the securities laws.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether securities-fraud plaintiffs can satisfy the PSLRA’s heightened pleading standards for scienter and falsity without pleading the contents of purported internal company documents and by relying on an expert opinion in place of particularized factual allegations.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 (PSLRA), especially 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(b)(1) (particularized pleading of misleading statement/omission) and § 78u-4(b)(2)(A) (particularized facts creating a strong inference of scienter).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: NVIDIA argues the PSLRA was enacted to curb abusive securities class actions by requiring plaintiffs to plead concrete, particularized facts at the complaint stage. When plaintiffs base scienter on alleged internal corporate documents, they must plead those documents’ contents with specificity—otherwise courts cannot evaluate whether the inference of scienter is “strong” as the statute requires. Likewise, plaintiffs cannot meet the PSLRA’s falsity requirement by substituting an expert’s say-so for detailed factual allegations showing what was false or misleading when said; allowing expert opinions to stand in for facts would dilute the PSLRA’s heightened pleading regime and invite fishing-expedition discovery and settlement pressure.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents contend the PSLRA does not impose a categorical requirement to plead verbatim or detailed contents of internal documents to plead scienter, and that complaints may rely on summarized internal information (e.g., accounts of internal reports, meetings, metrics, or communications) so long as the allegations, taken collectively, support a strong inference of scienter. They also argue expert analysis can be a proper part of pleading falsity—particularly where technical subject matter is involved—by explaining why challenged statements were misleading in context, without transforming the complaint into an evidentiary submission or requiring plaintiffs to have documentary proof before discovery.
key_precedents: Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith Inc. v. Dabit, 547 U.S. 71 (2006)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s access-to-justice concern is the hardest point: the PSLRA does not say “quote the documents,” and the discovery stay means plaintiffs often cannot. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson effectively concede, Tellabs’s comparative-inference inquiry cannot be performed on an expert’s bottom-line characterization or a generic invocation of “internal reports”; the complaint must plead concrete substance—what the internal information conveyed, when, to whom, and how it contradicts the public statements—so the court is weighing facts rather than labels. Dabit’s account of Congress’s design reinforces that this pre-discovery screening function must be meaningful, and the narrowest text-tethered rule is no categorical verbatim/attachment requirement, but a rigorously enforced particularity requirement sufficient to make Tellabs workable. That approach answers the access concern without rewriting §§ 78u-4(b)(1)–(2) into a permissive, document-free pleading regime that reintroduces the discovery leverage Congress aimed to curb.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s access-to-information concern is the strongest counterpoint: the PSLRA does not say “quote the document,” and the discovery stay makes verbatim pleading hard. But under the enacted text—plaintiffs must “specify” each misleading statement and “state with particularity facts” giving rise to a “strong inference”—a complaint that turns on internal reports must allege their concrete substance (what was conveyed, when, to whom, and how it contradicts the public statements), not merely characterize “internal documents” or outsource the factual predicate to an expert, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize. Tellabs’s holistic weighing presupposes pleaded facts adequate to compare culpable and nonculpable inferences; allowing generalized summaries untethered to specific internal contents would make that comparison impossible and would, as Justice Alito notes, recreate the discovery-driven leverage Congress targeted. Dabit’s account of the PSLRA’s purpose confirms the point of this heightened screen before discovery, and nothing in those precedents authorizes diluting the statutory particularity requirement into conclusory pleading.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan are correct that the PSLRA does not demand verbatim quotations and that the discovery stay makes that unrealistic in many cases, so I reject any categorical “quote-the-document” rule. But their access-to-justice framing does not answer the core textual and structural point Chief Justice Roberts presses: §§ 78u-4(b)(1)–(2) require plaintiffs to “specify” and “state with particularity” facts, and Tellabs’s comparative-inference test cannot be performed if the complaint substitutes generalized characterizations or an expert’s bottom line for concrete substance about what the internal reports conveyed, when, to whom, and how that contradicts the public statements. Dabit reinforces Congress’s purpose to prevent discovery-driven settlement leverage; allowing conclusory summaries of undisclosed internal materials would erode that gatekeeping function and effectively recreate the very dynamic the statute targeted. I can accept Justice Kagan’s “detailed summaries” only as a label for fact-like particulars that enable Tellabs, not as permission for nonfalsifiable descriptions that leave innocent inferences impossible to weigh.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito are right that Tellabs cannot be applied if plaintiffs merely gesture at “internal documents” or offer an expert’s ipse dixit; § 78u-4(b)(1)–(2) requires concrete substance (what, when, who, and the contradiction) to support a strong inference. But I do not read their workability concern to justify an extra-textual, quasi-document-production prerequisite that in practice demands near-verbatim internal contents despite the PSLRA discovery stay and issuers’ control of the most probative materials. Justice Kagan’s “substance, timing, linkage” framing captures the proper, text-tethered line: enforce rigorous particularity by requiring detailed, nonconclusory summaries tied to defendants’ knowledge, while rejecting generic invocations and expert bottom lines. Dabit supports Congress’s aim to curb abusive, discovery-driven suits, yet that purpose is satisfied by policing conclusory pleading—not by adopting a rule that predictably forecloses meritorious claims where plaintiffs can plead specifics without possessing the underlying documents.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett persuasively emphasize that Tellabs’s comparative “cogent and at least as compelling” inquiry is impossible if plaintiffs merely invoke “internal documents” or offer expert ipse dixit; I agree courts must demand concrete, nonconclusory substance. But that workability concern is fully satisfied by the PSLRA’s own text—§ 78u-4(b)(1) requiring plaintiffs to “specify” the misleading statements and “the reason or reasons why,” and § 78u-4(b)(2)(A) requiring particularized facts supporting a “strong inference”—without effectively converting pleading into a quasi-document-production rule that Congress did not enact and that, given the discovery stay, would skew against meritorious claims. Justice Alito’s discovery-leverage worry is real, yet it is better addressed by policing whether the complaint pleads fact-like summaries (what the internal metrics/report said, when it was communicated, to whom, and the contradiction) rather than by insisting on near-verbatim contents or attachments as a gatekeeping prerequisite. Dabit’s purpose to curb abusive suits supports rigor in applying particularity, not adding an extra-textual categorical requirement that displaces the statute’s calibrated pleading demands.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor rightly emphasize that the PSLRA nowhere demands verbatim quotations and that Tellabs requires a holistic, comparative assessment—but that point does not answer what § 78u-4(b)(1)–(2) positively requires: pleaded “facts” stated “with particularity” that allow a court to test competing inferences without speculation. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito stress, where falsity/scienter turns on internal reports, plaintiffs must allege the concrete substance (what the information conveyed, when, to whom, and how it contradicts the public statement), not merely characterize unseen materials or rely on an expert’s bottom-line; otherwise the Tellabs inquiry becomes unmoored and the PSLRA discovery stay is effectively circumvented. Dabit’s account of Congress’s design—to curb discovery-driven leverage—reinforces enforcing this textual gatekeeping function as written, while still rejecting any categorical “quote-or-lose” rule. Justice Sotomayor’s access-to-justice concern is substantial, but under a textualist approach it cannot justify relaxing “state with particularity facts” into a regime where conclusions substitute for pleaded facts whenever the issuer holds the documents.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan are right that the PSLRA does not impose a categorical verbatim-quotation rule and that Tellabs requires a holistic analysis; I would not graft a quasi-document-production requirement onto § 78u-4(b). But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito correctly emphasize that when falsity or scienter hinges on “internal reports/metrics,” §§ 78u-4(b)(1)–(2) still demand particularized, fact-like substance—what the internal information conveyed, when, to whom, and how it contradicts the public statement—so the court can do Tellabs’s comparative inference inquiry in a disciplined way rather than accept characterizations. Justice Jackson’s point about experts is useful as a limiting principle, yet expert analysis cannot substitute for pleading the predicate facts about defendants’ knowledge without undermining the PSLRA’s discovery-stay and gatekeeping design recognized in Dabit. On my institutionalist approach, the workable line is narrow and text-tethered: no verbatim requirement, but a meaningful particularity requirement for internal-source allegations to prevent Tellabs from becoming unmoored and the PSLRA from being circumvented.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan make the strongest point that the PSLRA does not textually require verbatim quotations and the discovery stay can limit access to underlying documents, so courts should not invent a quasi-production rule. But the statute’s own words—“specify” each misleading statement and “state with particularity facts” and “the reason or reasons why”—still demand enough concrete substance about internal materials (content, timing, audience, and the specific contradiction) to allow the Tellabs comparative-inference analysis to function as Congress designed, rather than accepting characterizations or expert ipse dixit. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on the discovery stay reinforces that Congress expected this screening to occur before discovery, which is defeated if plaintiffs can plead around particularity by invoking unseen internal reports without describing their substantive import in a fact-like way. Dabit’s account of the PSLRA’s purpose does not justify extra-textual hurdles, but it does confirm that rigorous application of the heightened pleading standard is essential precisely in the internal-information cases most likely to generate discovery leverage.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito are right that Tellabs cannot be administered on “internal reports show X” characterizations or expert ipse dixit; the complaint must supply concrete, falsifiable particulars sufficient to let courts weigh culpable and nonculpable inferences. But that concern is fully addressed by a demanding requirement of pleaded substance, timing, audience, and contradiction (as Justice Kagan frames it), without drifting into a de facto rule that plaintiffs must plead internal document contents at near-verbatim granularity despite the PSLRA discovery stay. Justice Barrett’s textual emphasis on “state with particularity” supports rigor in facts-and-reasons pleading, not an extra-textual prerequisite that predictably bars potentially meritorious claims where issuers uniquely control the underlying materials. Under a progressive, procedure-centered pragmatism, the workable line targets conclusory allegations and untethered experts while preserving fair access to court where plaintiffs can plead detailed summaries tied to specific meetings, metrics, and recipients.

John Roberts.reasoning: The PSLRA requires plaintiffs to “specify each statement alleged to have been misleading” and “the reason or reasons why,” and to “state with particularity facts giving rise to a strong inference” of scienter. 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(b)(1), (b)(2)(A). Under Tellabs, the inference of scienter must be “cogent and at least as compelling as any opposing inference,” which a court cannot reliably assess when the complaint invokes unspecified “internal documents” or substitutes an expert’s conclusion for particularized factual allegations tied to what defendants knew and when. 551 U.S. 308, 314 (2007). A narrow holding enforcing particularity where plaintiffs premise falsity or scienter on internal materials best respects Congress’s design to screen weak claims at the pleading stage and protects institutional legitimacy by adhering to the statute’s text and the PSLRA’s discovery-stay structure (§ 78u-4(b)(3)(B)).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The PSLRA’s text requires that a complaint “specify each statement alleged to have been misleading” and “the reason or reasons why the statement is misleading,” 15 U.S.C. § 78u-4(b)(1), and must “state with particularity facts giving rise to a strong inference” of scienter, § 78u-4(b)(2)(A). Under a textual reading, “particularity” and the comparative “strong inference” standard described in Tellabs demand concrete factual allegations that permit courts to weigh competing inferences at the pleading stage, not generalized references to undisclosed internal documents or an expert’s conclusory say-so. Allowing scienter and falsity to be pled without the substance of the alleged internal materials would dilute Congress’s deliberate tightening of pleading and enable the very discovery-driven suits the PSLRA sought to curb. Accordingly, plaintiffs who premise fraud on internal company information must plead that information with sufficient specificity to make the Tellabs inference analysis meaningful and to satisfy § 78u-4(b)(1) and (b)(2)(A).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The PSLRA’s text requires plaintiffs to “specify each statement alleged to have been misleading” and “the reason or reasons why,” § 78u-4(b)(1), and to “state with particularity facts giving rise to a strong inference” of scienter, § 78u-4(b)(2)(A). If scienter is premised on supposed internal documents, a complaint that withholds their contents and offers only generalized characterizations deprives courts of the ability to perform the comparative inference analysis Tellabs demands—i.e., whether the inference of fraud is “cogent and at least as compelling” as nonfraudulent explanations.
